screens.title: Amazon SNS — Simple Notification Service
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what Amazon SNS provides and why you would choose it when building event-driven systems. SNS implements the publish/subscribe model: a producer publishes a message to a topic and SNS reliably delivers that single message to all subscribed endpoints. This fan-out capability is ideal when one event must trigger many independent actions — for example notifying inventory, payments, and analytics after an order is placed. We will examine topic structure, subscriber types like SQS and Lambda, message attributes and filter policies, and the access controls that keep topics secure. You will also see a live-style code walkthrough using the AWS SDK for Python to create topics, subscribe an SQS queue, publish messages with attributes, and verify delivery. By the end you should understand how SNS decouples producers from consumers, how filtering reduces unnecessary processing, and the common permission mistake to avoid when connecting SNS to SQS. Think of SNS as a dispatcher that sends the same bulletin to many recipients while letting each recipient choose which bulletins to accept.

screens.title: Publish/Subscribe Model and SNS
screens.narratorSegment: Publish/subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders emit messages to an intermediary and receivers subscribe to that intermediary to get messages. In Amazon SNS, that intermediary is a topic: publishers send messages to a topic and SNS delivers them to every subscribed endpoint. This decouples the sending application from the set of receivers, so the publisher does not need to manage endpoints or worry about delivery logic. A concrete example is an e-commerce 'Order Placed' event. The order service publishes the event to a topic. Inventory updates, payment reconciliation, and analytics all subscribe to that topic and receive the same event simultaneously. A common misconception is to treat SNS like a queue — but unlike a queue that hands each message to a single consumer, SNS fans out one message to many subscribers. This matters because your choice affects delivery semantics: use SNS when multiple consumers need the same event, and use SQS when you want one worker per message. Key takeaway: SNS centralizes broadcasting while leaving each subscriber responsibility for processing and reliability. Publish/Subscribe Model and SNS means publishers push to a topic; sns distributes that message to all subscribers, enabling decoupled broadcast.. In practical terms, definition and why pub/sub helps decouple services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Pub/Sub Definition
What pub/sub means

Publishers, Topic, Subscribers

A publisher emits a message to a topic. The topic is a logical channel. Subscribers register to receive messages published to that topic.

Example
An Order Placed event is published once and delivered to inventory, payment, and analytics systems.
Misconception
SNS is not a point-to-point queue. Use SQS when each message must be consumed by only one worker.
Key Takeaway

Choose SNS for broadcasting the same event to multiple independent consumers; choose SQS for single-consumer work distribution.

Visual analogy
Dispatcher analogy
Think of SNS as a dispatcher that posts a single bulletin and every subscribed office copies it for their own work.
Check your understanding
  • Why would you use SNS instead of SQS?
  • What changes if subscribers use SQS queues behind SNS?

screens.title: SNS Topic, Publisher, and Subscriber Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: SNS sits between publishers and subscribers as a managed intermediary. The core component is the topic, which is the logical channel that receives publishes. Publishers only need the topic ARN; they do not need to know about endpoints. Subscribers register to a topic using a protocol such as SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, email, SMS, or mobile push. When a message is published, SNS performs the fan-out: it delivers the message to each subscriber using the protocol they chose. A common architecture pattern is SNS → multiple SQS queues. This provides durable storage and allows each consumer group to process at its own pace. Another pattern is SNS → Lambda for immediate serverless processing of events. Important practical detail: when subscribing an SQS queue, the queue's resource policy must permit sns. amazonaws. com to send messages and often restrict the source ARN to the topic. Without that policy change, subscriptions may appear but messages will not be delivered. Think of the topic as the directory listing that routes copies of a memo to many inboxes. SNS Topic, Publisher, and Subscriber Architecture means a topic decouples publishers and subscribers; subscribers can be queues, functions, endpoints, or user channels, and each receives its own copy of the message.. In practical terms, how components connect and the fan-out path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Architecture & Fan-out
Core elements
  • Topic: logical access point and ARN.
  • Publisher: any service that calls SNS publish with an ARN.
  • Subscriber: endpoint registered for delivery via a protocol.
Pattern: Fan-out to SQS
Useful when each consumer group needs durable delivery and independent processing speed.
Pattern: SNS to Lambda
Great for immediate serverless reactions such as notifications or lightweight processing.
Concrete scenario
Use case
On order placement, publish an 'Order Placed' message to a topic. The inventory service reads from an SQS queue subscribed to the topic, the billing system receives through Lambda, and analytics receive via HTTP endpoint.
Gotcha
If the SQS queue policy doesn’t allow SNS to send messages, delivery will silently fail even with an active subscription.

screens.title: Subscriber Types & Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: SNS supports many subscriber types, and choosing the right one depends on delivery guarantees and processing needs. SQS queues are commonly used when you need durability and the ability to retry processing—publishers send to a topic and the queue stores messages until workers consume them. Lambda subscribers are ideal for small, immediate serverless tasks; SNS invokes the function directly. HTTP/S endpoints work when an external service needs to receive the message via POST; that endpoint must handle retries and authentication. Email and SMS are for user-facing notifications where direct delivery to a person is desired. Mobile push targets device platforms for app notifications. A concrete example: for an e-commerce flow, send order events to an SQS queue for batch fulfillment jobs, to a Lambda for fraud checks, and to an HTTP analytics endpoint for real-time dashboards. A common mistake is using email or SMS for high-volume business events; these channels are meant for human notifications and can be costly or rate-limited. The takeaway: match subscriber type to processing needs and expected throughput. Subscriber Types & Use Cases means pick sqs for durability and independent consumers, lambda for serverless triggers, http/s for external services, and human channels for notifications.. In practical terms, sqs, lambda, http/s, email, sms, mobile push — when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SQS
Durable queue for asynchronous processing and retry logic. Use when you need reliable, decoupled consumers.
Lambda
Immediate serverless invocation for short processing tasks and event-driven logic.
HTTP/S
Deliver messages via POST to external services or webhooks that can handle retries.

screens.title: Message Attributes and Filtering
screens.narratorSegment: Message attributes let you attach structured metadata to a published message, and they are central to SNS filter policies. Attributes are key-value pairs that travel with the message but are separate from the message body. Subscribers can specify a filter policy that describes which attribute values they want. For example, if an 'Order Placed' topic includes an attribute named order_type with values like 'premium' or 'standard', one subscriber can receive only 'premium' orders by defining a filter for that attribute. This reduces unnecessary processing and avoids building custom routing inside subscribers. A common mistake is relying on message body parsing in subscribers instead of using attributes and filter policies; attributes are more efficient because SNS filters before delivery. When designing filter policies, be explicit and test: publish messages with different attributes and confirm that subscribers only receive matching messages. Takeaway: use message attributes to express routing logic and keep subscribers focused on processing the messages they care about. Message Attributes and Filtering means use message attributes and filter policies to let sns perform routing so subscribers get only relevant messages.. In practical terms, add metadata and route messages with filter policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Attributes & Filters
Message attributes

Attach key-value metadata that SNS can evaluate for delivery decisions without the subscriber parsing the body.

Example attributes
EventType: OrderPlaced, Region: us-east-1, Priority: 1
Filter policy example
{"order_type": ["premium"]}
Why filtering helps
  • Reduces unnecessary processing by subscribers.
  • Lets SNS do routing decisions at delivery time.
  • Makes subscribers simpler and more focused.
Check

screens.title: Access Policies and Security for Topics
screens.narratorSegment: SNS topics use access policies to control permissions; these are IAM-style policies attached directly to the topic. Typical permissions include sns:Publish to allow a principal to send messages and sns:Subscribe to allow subscriptions. The principle of least privilege applies: grant only the principals that need permission. A common real-world mistake is leaving topic policies too permissive, which can let unauthorized principals publish or subscribe. When integrating with SQS, also consider the SQS queue's resource policy: you must allow the SNS service principal to perform sqs:SendMessage on the queue and usually add a condition that aws:SourceArn equals the SNS topic ARN. Otherwise the subscription will not result in actual message delivery. Test policies by attempting a publish from an allowed principal and from a disallowed principal to confirm enforcement. The takeaway is to design topic and queue policies together so the end-to-end flow is secure and functional. Access Policies and Security for Topics means apply least-privilege topic policies and ensure sqs queue policies explicitly allow sns to send messages from the topic arn.. In practical terms, control who can publish and who can subscribe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Access Policies
Topic policy purpose

Define which principals can publish and which can subscribe to a topic. Use explicit allow statements and limit principals by ARN when possible.

Common permissions
  • sns:Publish
  • sns:Subscribe
SQS queue policy

Grant the SNS service permission to send messages to the queue and add a condition restricting aws:SourceArn to the topic ARN.

Policy snippet
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": {"Service": "sns.amazonaws.com"},
    "Action": "SQS:SendMessage",
    "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:...:OrderProcessingQueue",
    "Condition": {"ArnEquals": {"aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:...:OrderEventsTopic"}}
  }]
}

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Create & Subscribe
Key calls
sns = boto3.client('sns')
sqs = boto3.client('sqs')

response = sns.create_topic(Name='OrderEventsTopic')

screens.narratorSegment: After wiring SNS and SQS, publish a message with attributes to test delivery and filtering. In Boto3 you call sns. publish with the TopicArn, a Message body, a Subject, and a MessageAttributes map. Use attributes to carry routing metadata like EventType or Priority. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Publish & Verify
Publish example
message_data = { "orderId": "ORD-001", "customerName": "Alice Smith", "totalAmount": 99.99 }

response = sns.publish(
  TopicArn=topic_arn,
  Message=json.dumps(message_data),
  Subject='New Order Notification',
  MessageAttributes={
    'EventType': {'DataType': 'String', 'StringValue': 'OrderPlaced'},
    'Region': {'DataType': 'String', 'StringValue': 'us-east-1'},
    'Priority': {'DataType': 'Number', 'StringValue': '1'}
  }
)
print(response['MessageId'])
Receive & inspect
resp = sqs.receive_message(QueueUrl=queue_url, MaxNumberOfMessages=1, WaitTimeSeconds=10)
messages = resp.get('Messages', [])
if messages:
  sns_message = json.loads(messages[0]['Body'])
  print(sns_message['Subject'])
  print(sns_message['Message'])
  sqs.delete_message(QueueUrl=queue_url, ReceiptHandle=messages[0]['ReceiptHandle'])
Note

SNS wraps the original payload inside the SQS message body. Parse that wrapper to find the original Message and MessageAttributes.

screens.title: Pitfalls, Troubleshooting, and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: When working with SNS, several recurring issues are worth watching for. First, forgetting to set the SQS queue resource policy to allow sns. amazonaws. com is the most common reason messages don’t arrive; subscriptions may exist but delivery will fail without the proper queue policy. Second, treating SNS like a queue leads to incorrect design decisions: SNS delivers copies to every subscriber, so if you need only one consumer per message, use SQS. Third, not using message attributes and filter policies results in inefficient subscribers that receive irrelevant messages. Fourth, overly permissive topic policies can allow unintended principals to publish or subscribe; always restrict principals and test deny scenarios. For troubleshooting, publish test messages with clear attributes, check subscription ARNs, and inspect SQS queue metrics and Lambda logs. Best practice: design your topic, subscription filters, and queue policies together so security, routing, and delivery are consistent from publish to processing. A final question to reflect on: how would you design filter policies to minimize Lambda invocations for low-priority events? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what Amazon SNS provides and why you would choose it when building event-driven systems. SNS implements the publish/subscribe model: a producer publishes a message to a topic and SNS reliably delivers that single message to all subscribed endpoints. This fan-out capability is ideal when one event must trigger many independent actions — for example notifying inventory, payments, and analytics after an order is placed. We will examine topic structure, subscriber types like SQS and Lambda, message attributes and filter policies, and the access controls that keep topics secure. You will also see a live-style code walkthrough using the AWS SDK for Python to create topics, subscribe an SQS queue, publish messages with attributes, and verify delivery. By the end you should understand how SNS decouples producers from consumers, how filtering reduces unnecessary processing, and the common permission mistake to avoid when connecting SNS to SQS. Think of SNS as a dispatcher that sends the same bulletin to many recipients while letting each recipient choose which bulletins to accept.

In this chapter we set clear, practical learning objectives so you leave with usable skills. First, you will be able to explain the publish/subscribe model and how SNS implements it. That means recognizing why a topic decouples the sender from many receivers, and being able to describe fan-out in your own architecture diagrams. Second, you will identify the common subscriber types — SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, email, SMS, and mobile push — and match them to use cases like reliable processing, serverless triggers, or user notifications. Third, you will implement publishing messages with the AWS SDK for Python; you should be able to create a topic, subscribe an endpoint, and publish a message with attributes. Finally, you will configure topic access policies and message filter policies to control who publishes and which subscribers receive which messages. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you know when you’ve achieved competency and can apply SNS safely in production.

This second objectives screen explains how to verify and practice the skills you'll learn. For explaining pub/sub, draw an architecture where a single publisher sends an 'Order Placed' event to a topic and three subscribers receive it: an SQS queue for processing, a Lambda for immediate work, and an HTTP endpoint for analytics. For subscriber identification, build a short mapping table that lists each subscriber type and a one-line use case. To verify SDK proficiency, perform the create-topic, subscribe, publish, and receive flow with Boto3 and confirm the message appears in your SQS queue or your Lambda logs. Finally, for policies and filters, create a conservative topic policy that grants sns:Publish only to specific principals and add a subscription filter policy that matches a message attribute. Each verification step should be repeatable in a sandbox account so you can demonstrate the competency milestone in minutes.

Publish/subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders emit messages to an intermediary and receivers subscribe to that intermediary to get messages. In Amazon SNS, that intermediary is a topic: publishers send messages to a topic and SNS delivers them to every subscribed endpoint. This decouples the sending application from the set of receivers, so the publisher does not need to manage endpoints or worry about delivery logic. A concrete example is an e-commerce 'Order Placed' event. The order service publishes the event to a topic. Inventory updates, payment reconciliation, and analytics all subscribe to that topic and receive the same event simultaneously. A common misconception is to treat SNS like a queue — but unlike a queue that hands each message to a single consumer, SNS fans out one message to many subscribers. This matters because your choice affects delivery semantics: use SNS when multiple consumers need the same event, and use SQS when you want one worker per message. Key takeaway: SNS centralizes broadcasting while leaving each subscriber responsibility for processing and reliability. Publish/Subscribe Model and SNS means publishers push to a topic; sns distributes that message to all subscribers, enabling decoupled broadcast.. In practical terms, definition and why pub/sub helps decouple services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SNS sits between publishers and subscribers as a managed intermediary. The core component is the topic, which is the logical channel that receives publishes. Publishers only need the topic ARN; they do not need to know about endpoints. Subscribers register to a topic using a protocol such as SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, email, SMS, or mobile push. When a message is published, SNS performs the fan-out: it delivers the message to each subscriber using the protocol they chose. A common architecture pattern is SNS → multiple SQS queues. This provides durable storage and allows each consumer group to process at its own pace. Another pattern is SNS → Lambda for immediate serverless processing of events. Important practical detail: when subscribing an SQS queue, the queue's resource policy must permit sns. amazonaws. com to send messages and often restrict the source ARN to the topic. Without that policy change, subscriptions may appear but messages will not be delivered. Think of the topic as the directory listing that routes copies of a memo to many inboxes. SNS Topic, Publisher, and Subscriber Architecture means a topic decouples publishers and subscribers; subscribers can be queues, functions, endpoints, or user channels, and each receives its own copy of the message.. In practical terms, how components connect and the fan-out path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SNS supports many subscriber types, and choosing the right one depends on delivery guarantees and processing needs. SQS queues are commonly used when you need durability and the ability to retry processing—publishers send to a topic and the queue stores messages until workers consume them. Lambda subscribers are ideal for small, immediate serverless tasks; SNS invokes the function directly. HTTP/S endpoints work when an external service needs to receive the message via POST; that endpoint must handle retries and authentication. Email and SMS are for user-facing notifications where direct delivery to a person is desired. Mobile push targets device platforms for app notifications. A concrete example: for an e-commerce flow, send order events to an SQS queue for batch fulfillment jobs, to a Lambda for fraud checks, and to an HTTP analytics endpoint for real-time dashboards. A common mistake is using email or SMS for high-volume business events; these channels are meant for human notifications and can be costly or rate-limited. The takeaway: match subscriber type to processing needs and expected throughput. Subscriber Types & Use Cases means pick sqs for durability and independent consumers, lambda for serverless triggers, http/s for external services, and human channels for notifications.. In practical terms, sqs, lambda, http/s, email, sms, mobile push — when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Message attributes let you attach structured metadata to a published message, and they are central to SNS filter policies. Attributes are key-value pairs that travel with the message but are separate from the message body. Subscribers can specify a filter policy that describes which attribute values they want. For example, if an 'Order Placed' topic includes an attribute named order_type with values like 'premium' or 'standard', one subscriber can receive only 'premium' orders by defining a filter for that attribute. This reduces unnecessary processing and avoids building custom routing inside subscribers. A common mistake is relying on message body parsing in subscribers instead of using attributes and filter policies; attributes are more efficient because SNS filters before delivery. When designing filter policies, be explicit and test: publish messages with different attributes and confirm that subscribers only receive matching messages. Takeaway: use message attributes to express routing logic and keep subscribers focused on processing the messages they care about. Message Attributes and Filtering means use message attributes and filter policies to let sns perform routing so subscribers get only relevant messages.. In practical terms, add metadata and route messages with filter policies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SNS topics use access policies to control permissions; these are IAM-style policies attached directly to the topic. Typical permissions include sns:Publish to allow a principal to send messages and sns:Subscribe to allow subscriptions. The principle of least privilege applies: grant only the principals that need permission. A common real-world mistake is leaving topic policies too permissive, which can let unauthorized principals publish or subscribe. When integrating with SQS, also consider the SQS queue's resource policy: you must allow the SNS service principal to perform sqs:SendMessage on the queue and usually add a condition that aws:SourceArn equals the SNS topic ARN. Otherwise the subscription will not result in actual message delivery. Test policies by attempting a publish from an allowed principal and from a disallowed principal to confirm enforcement. The takeaway is to design topic and queue policies together so the end-to-end flow is secure and functional. Access Policies and Security for Topics means apply least-privilege topic policies and ensure sqs queue policies explicitly allow sns to send messages from the topic arn.. In practical terms, control who can publish and who can subscribe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll walk through the key Boto3 operations for wiring SNS to SQS. First, create the SNS client and call create_topic with a name. That returns a TopicArn used by publishers and subscribers. Then create an SQS queue and get its QueueArn. When working with SNS, several recurring issues are worth watching for. First, forgetting to set the SQS queue resource policy to allow sns. amazonaws. com is the most common reason messages don’t arrive; subscriptions may exist but delivery will fail without the proper queue policy. Second, treating SNS like a queue leads to incorrect design decisions: SNS delivers copies to every subscriber, so if you need only one consumer per message, use SQS. Third, not using message attributes and filter policies results in inefficient subscribers that receive irrelevant messages. Fourth, overly permissive topic policies can allow unintended principals to publish or subscribe; always restrict principals and test deny scenarios. For troubleshooting, publish test messages with clear attributes, check subscription ARNs, and inspect SQS queue metrics and Lambda logs. Best practice: design your topic, subscription filters, and queue policies together so security, routing, and delivery are consistent from publish to processing. Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, the publish/subscribe model: SNS acts as an intermediary topic that lets publishers broadcast messages without knowing subscribers. This decoupling simplifies architecture and enables fan-out. Second, SNS supports many subscriber types like SQS and Lambda; choose SQS for durable, asynchronous processing and Lambda for immediate serverless work. Third, message attributes and filter policies let subscribers receive only the messages they care about. Use attributes for routing metadata and apply filter policies to reduce unnecessary processing. As a security reminder, always apply least-privilege topic policies and confirm SQS queue policies allow SNS to send messages. Keep these core ideas in mind as you design event-driven systems with SNS.
